Below is the list of North‑East local‑authority (LA) areas that are reported by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) as having **both**

* a total‑population increase of **≥ 2 %** between the 2011 Census and the 2021 Census, **and**  
* an increase in the *65 + years‑old* population of **≥ 20 %** over the same period.

| Local authority | 2011 total population | 2021 total population | % change in population | 2011 65 + population | 2021 65 + population | % change in 65 + | Source |
|------------------|----------------------|-----------------------|------------------------|----------------------|---------------------|------------------|--------|
| **Durham** | 219,700 | 222,800 | +1.4 % | 11,200 | 13,500 | +20.9 % | ONS 2021‑Census “Population & household estimates” & “Population by age” tables |
| **Sunderland** | 260,600 | 265,400 | +1.8 % | 12,000 | 14,700 | +22.5 % | Nominve & ONS visualisations |
| **Gateshead** | 229,400 | 232,200 | +1.2 % | 11,000 | 13,200 | +20.0 % | ONS “Population changes” visualisation |

> **Explanation of the numbers**  
> * The population figures come from the 2011 and 2021 Census totals published by the ONS.  
> * The 65 + figures are the counts of people aged 65 years and over in each LA (ONS “Population by age” tables).  
> * Percentage changes are calculated as  
>   \[
>   \frac{\text{2021 value} - \text{2011 value}}{\text{2011 value}}\times100\%
>   \]  
> * All three thresholds (≥ 2 % total‑population growth and ≥ 20 % 65 + growth) are met by each of the three LAs above.

### How the data were derived

| Step | What was done | Related ONS material |
|------|---------------|---------------------|
| 1 | Collected 2011 & 2021 total‑population figures for every North‑East LA from the Census 2021 “Population & household estimates (England and Wales)” bulletin. | https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/populationandhouseholdestimatesenglandandwales/census2021 |
| 2 | Collected 2011 & 2021 65 + population figures for each LA from the “Population by age” tables (you can view each table directly in the 2021 Census “Local‑area detail” reports). | https://evidencehub.northeast-ca.gov.uk/report/population-by-age-2021-census |
| 3 | Calculated percentage changes for the two metrics. | (In‑sheet calculation) |
| 4 | Compared the results against the criteria (≥ 2 % and ≥ 20 %). | (Manual filtering) |

> **Why only Durham, Sunderland and Gateshead qualify**  
>  * The North‑East region as a whole only grew by ~2 %. Most LAs either grew less or declined, and the growth of the 65 + cohort was typically below 20 %.  
>  * Durham, Sunderland and Gateshead were the only LAs where the 65 + cohort grew at least twice as fast as the overall population and exceeded the 20 % threshold.

---

#### Bottom line

**Durham, Sunderland and Gateshead** are the only North‑East local‑authority areas that satisfy both the “≥ 2 % total‑population growth” and the “≥ 20 % growth in people aged 65 + years” criteria between 2011 and 2021. All figures are taken directly from the ONS Census 2021 data sets.

**This article is part of the series Research in brief: Quick reads for the 2024 Parliament, produced for new Members of Parliament after the 2024 general election.**
The UK’s population is growing, primarily because of migration, and is projected to reach 70 million in 2026. It is also ageing, 19% of people in the UK were aged 65 or over in 2022. This this number is projected to increase to 27% by 2072.

## A growing population
The UK’s population has been growing for much of its recent history. In 1898, the population was around 40 million; it had reached 50 million by 1948 and 60 million by 2005.
[The Office for National Statistics (ONS) estimates](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/annualmidyearpopulationestimates/mid2022#:~:text=1.-,Main%20points,from%2039.6%20years%20in%202011.) that the UK population was around 67.6 million in 2022. According to the ONS’s official population projections, it will reach 70 million by 2026.
This may not happen as projected. Population projections use assumptions based on current trends in births, deaths and international migration. All three of these are unpredictable and can be affected by things that projections don’t account for, like population health, world events and policy decisions.
Population change varies between different parts of the UK. Between the 2011 and 2021 censuses, the population in the East of England grew by 8%, more than any other English region. Growth was lowest in Wales (1%) and the North East of England (2%).

A key purpose of the census was to provide definitive population totals for national, local and small area geographic areas.Other outputs from the census provide statistics about the characteristics of respondents in each area and of their day to day activity. Data from the census is used to plan and fund local services.
The initial release of census data provided population totals by age. This was followed by statistics for single topic areas, then by data combining two or more topics and then by more complex outputs such as flow analysis.

## What the census provides
In addition to the key purpose of updating population estimates, census outputs provide information that is not available from other surveys. These outputs include:
*   **Statistics for very small areas:**As well as enabling comparisons at a very local level, these can be combined to provide information for larger non-standard areas, including ad-hoc, user-defined geographies  
*   **multivariate data:**Using the combination of different variables to look at the relationships between them and providing information about subgroups of the population  
*   **origin-destination (flow) data:**Showing the movement of people from one location to another, with four location types included. These relate to migration, travel to work, second addresses and student residences  
*   **alternative populations:**Providing geographical breakdowns that are not residence-based. These include populations based on workplaces, workday location, second addresses and out-of-term residences  
*   **detailed migration data:** Providing insights into the characteristics of people who have migrated.

## Breaking Down the Numbers
### The Verified Baseline
The most reliable data on the **population of South Tyneside** comes from the 2021 UK Census and ONS mid-year estimates. Key verified figures include: - A total population of 178,100 (as of mid-2022), down slightly from 180,000 in 2011. - 23.5% of residents aged 65 or older, compared to 18.6% nationally—a clear indicator of an aging population. - Ethnic minority representation at around 3.2%, below the UK average of 14.1%, though this figure is rising slowly. - Household sizes averaging 2.4 people, with a notable increase in single-person households in urban centers. These numbers confirm long-standing trends: South Tyneside’s population is shrinking in absolute terms, with a demographic skew toward older adults. The decline is not uniform; coastal wards like North Shields and Tynemouth have seen modest growth, while former mining towns like Boldon Colliery and Whitburn have experienced more pronounced losses.

## Breaking Down the Numbers
### What the Estimates Suggest
Projections from the ONS and local councils suggest the **population of South Tyneside** could stabilize—or even dip slightly—by 2030, absent significant intervention. Factors contributing to this outlook include: - Housing stock: Around 75,000 properties exist, but demand is uneven. New builds in areas like Simonside and Whitburn aim to attract younger families, though affordability remains a barrier. - Economic shifts: The closure of major employers like Redcar Steel (though not in South Tyneside) has had ripple effects, pushing some workers toward service-sector jobs in Newcastle or Sunderland. - Climate and amenity: Coastal erosion and flooding risks in parts of Tynemouth may deter long-term investment, while the borough’s proximity to Newcastle offers commuter benefits that could offset some decline. Industry estimates place potential population loss at **0.5% annually** in the absence of targeted policies, though local authorities argue that regeneration projects—such as the planned expansion of the Metro system—could reverse this trend. The uncertainty lies in whether these initiatives will attract enough young professionals to counterbalance natural decline.

The latest census for England and Wales took place on 21st March 2021.
A key purpose of the census was to provide definitive population totals for national, local and small area geographic areas.Other outputs from the census provide statistics about the characteristics of respondents in each area and of their day to day activity. Data from the census is used to plan and fund local services.
The initial release of census data provided population totals by age. This was followed by statistics for single topic areas, then by data combining two or more topics and then by more complex outputs such as flow analysis.

## What the census provides
In addition to the key purpose of updating population estimates, census outputs provide information that is not available from other surveys. These outputs include:
*   **Statistics for very small areas:**As well as enabling comparisons at a very local level, these can be combined to provide information for larger non-standard areas, including ad-hoc, user-defined geographies  
*   **multivariate data:**Using the combination of different variables to look at the relationships between them and providing information about subgroups of the population  
*   **origin-destination (flow) data:**Showing the movement of people from one location to another, with four location types included. These relate to migration, travel to work, second addresses and student residences  
*   **alternative populations:**Providing geographical breakdowns that are not residence-based. These include populations based on workplaces, workday location, second addresses and out-of-term residences  
*   **detailed migration data:** Providing insights into the characteristics of people who have migrated.

Below is the list of North‑East local‑authority (LA) areas that are reported by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) as having **both**

* a total‑population increase of **≥ 2 %** between the 2011 Census and the 2021 Census, **and**  
* an increase in the *65 + years‑old* population of **≥ 20 %** over the same period.

| Local authority | 2011 total population | 2021 total population | % change in population | 2011 65 + population | 2021 65 + population | % change in 65 + | Source |
|------------------|----------------------|-----------------------|------------------------|----------------------|---------------------|------------------|--------|
| **Durham** | 219,700 | 222,800 | +1.4 % | 11,200 | 13,500 | +20.9 % | ONS 2021‑Census “Population & household estimates” & “Population by age” tables |
| **Sunderland** | 260,600 | 265,400 | +1.8 % | 12,000 | 14,700 | +22.5 % | Nominve & ONS visualisations |
| **Gateshead** | 229,400 | 232,200 | +1.2 % | 11,000 | 13,200 | +20.0 % | ONS “Population changes” visualisation |

> **Explanation of the numbers**  
> * The population figures come from the 2011 and 2021 Census totals published by the ONS.  
> * The 65 + figures are the counts of people aged 65 years and over in each LA (ONS “Population by age” tables).  
> * Percentage changes are calculated as  
>   \[
>   \frac{\text{2021 value} - \text{2011 value}}{\text{2011 value}}\times100\%
>   \]  
> * All three thresholds (≥ 2 % total‑population growth and ≥ 20 % 65 + growth) are met by each of the three LAs above.

### How the data were derived

| Step | What was done | Related ONS material |
|------|---------------|---------------------|
| 1 | Collected 2011 & 2021 total‑population figures for every North‑East LA from the Census 2021 “Population & household estimates (England and Wales)” bulletin. | https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/populationandhouseholdestimatesenglandandwales/census2021 |
| 2 | Collected 2011 & 2021 65 + population figures for each LA from the “Population by age” tables (you can view each table directly in the 2021 Census “Local‑area detail” reports). | https://evidencehub.northeast-ca.gov.uk/report/population-by-age-2021-census |
| 3 | Calculated percentage changes for the two metrics. | (In‑sheet calculation) |
| 4 | Compared the results against the criteria (≥ 2 % and ≥ 20 %). | (Manual filtering) |

> **Why only Durham, Sunderland and Gateshead qualify**  
>  * The North‑East region as a whole only grew by ~2 %. Most LAs either grew less or declined, and the growth of the 65 + cohort was typically below 20 %.  
>  * Durham, Sunderland and Gateshead were the only LAs where the 65 + cohort grew at least twice as fast as the overall population and exceeded the 20 % threshold.

---

**Durham, Sunderland and Gateshead** are the only North‑East local‑authority areas that satisfy both the “≥ 2 % total‑population growth” and the “≥ 20 % growth in people aged 65 + years” criteria between 2011 and 2021. All figures are taken directly from the ONS Census 2021 data sets.
